name: Himachal
tagline: Cedar villages, travelling gods and apple country
meta_description: Plan Himachal: Shimla, Manali, Dharamshala, Bir, Parvati, Tirthan, Chamba and Kinnaur. Seasons, real INR costs, HRTC buses, stays and trips from saver to signature.
summary: Himachal is the easiest big mountain trip from Delhi: an overnight HRTC Volvo puts you in Shimla, Manali or Dharamshala for ₹900–1,900. Come March to June or late September to November. Budget ₹1,800–3,000 a day on hostels and buses, or far more for Oberoi rooms above Shimla.
intro: Our Himachal hive runs from the Shimla ridges to the Dhauladhar wall above Dharamshala, up the Beas through Kullu to Manali, east along the Sutlej into Kinnaur, and west into the old Chamba kingdom on the Ravi. Spiti and Lahaul, beyond the Rohtang and Kunzum passes, have their own hive. What ties this half of the state together is altitude in a friendly range: most towns sit between 1,000 and 2,200 m, so you sleep well, eat well and still look at 5,000–6,000 m peaks over breakfast.

It is also the best-connected part of the western Himalaya. Himachal Road Transport Corporation (HRTC) runs Volvo and ordinary buses from Delhi's Kashmere Gate ISBT to almost every town in this hive, and its red buses reach villages that have no other public transport. Three small airports, at Jubbarhatti near Shimla, Bhuntar near Kullu and Gaggal near Dharamshala, take short flights from Delhi. The narrow-gauge Kalka–Shimla Railway, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2008, is still a working line.

We plan Himachal around its villages rather than its malls. Kullu and Naggar keep kath-kuni houses of deodar and stone that ride out earthquakes. Each village has its devta, a deity carried in a palanquin to fairs and to the great Kullu Dussehra in October. Kinnaur grows apples and chilgoza pine nuts at 2,500–3,000 m, Chamba still embroiders its rumals, and the Tibetan community in McLeodganj has made upper Dharamshala a centre of Tibetan Buddhist learning since 1960.

Honest trade-offs: Shimla and Manali are crowded in May, June and the Christmas–New Year week, and hotel prices double. July and August bring monsoon landslides that close roads for hours or days, especially in Kullu and Kinnaur. Snow in January and February is beautiful in Manali and Shimla but can block the higher roads. Our favourite windows are April, early June, and the clear weeks from late September to mid-November.

chapters.heading: Houses that bend in an earthquake
chapters.text: Walk through Naggar or the upper Tirthan valley and the houses are striped: a course of deodar beam, a course of dry stone, then timber again, with no mortar holding them together. Builders call it kath-kuni, roughly 'wood and corner', because the beams lock at the corners. The weight of the stone holds the timber down, and the timber lets the wall flex and settle when the ground shakes. The 1905 Kangra earthquake killed about 20,000 people and flattened brick and masonry buildings in Dharamshala and Kangra. Kath-kuni temples and towers in Kullu still stand from centuries before that. The catch is the cedar: deodar is now protected and expensive, so many families build in concrete, and the old skill survives mostly through temple repairs and a handful of careful homestay builders.

chapters.heading: Gods who travel to the fair
chapters.text: In Kullu every village has a devta, a deity who owns land, settles disputes through an oracle called the gur, and travels. Villagers carry the devta's mask-covered palanquin, the rath, to fairs across the valley, with drums and long brass horns. The largest gathering is Kullu Dussehra. Its centre is Raghunath, a form of Rama whose idol Raja Jagat Singh installed in the 17th century, after which the king ruled in the god's name. Hundreds of village devtas come to Dhalpur ground in Kullu to pay respects, but the festival cannot begin until goddess Hadimba arrives from Manali. Malana, high in a side valley of the Parvati, follows its own deity, Jamlu, and runs its affairs through a village council. Visitors are asked not to touch its houses, temple or people, and we keep to that.

chapters.heading: A summer capital on a toy railway
chapters.text: In 1864 the British made Shimla the summer capital of India, and for the hot months the government of a subcontinent moved up a ridge at about 2,200 m. Everything had to come up by mule and cart until the 96 km narrow-gauge line from Kalka opened in 1903, climbing from about 650 m to 2,076 m through 102 tunnels. The longest, at Barog, is just over 1 km. The Viceregal Lodge, finished in 1888, now houses the Indian Institute of Advanced Study. UNESCO added the Kalka–Shimla Railway to the Mountain Railways of India World Heritage Site in 2008. It still runs several trains a day, and the slow ones are cheaper than a bus seat.

chapters.heading: Apples, wool and a home in exile
chapters.text: Himachal's apple economy has an unlikely origin. Samuel Evans Stokes, an American who settled at Kotgarh above the Sutlej, planted improved American apple varieties there in the early 20th century and showed hill farmers they could sell fruit rather than only grow grain. Orchards spread to Kullu, Shimla district and later Kinnaur, where apples now grow to around 3,000 m. Wool tells a similar story of trade: the Kullu shawl, woven on pit looms with bold geometric borders, now carries a Geographical Indication tag. And from 1960 the Dalai Lama and thousands of Tibetan refugees made upper Dharamshala their base, building temples, schools, archives and craft workshops that now draw students from around the world.

highlights.title: Ride the Kalka–Shimla toy train
highlights.text: Five to six hours, 102 tunnels and a climb of more than 1,400 m on a 2 ft 6 in gauge line opened in 1903. The ordinary trains cost less than a bus ticket; the Shivalik Deluxe and Vistadome cost more and need booking weeks ahead in season.

highlights.title: Sleep in a 15th-century castle
highlights.text: HPTDC runs Naggar Castle, a kath-kuni fort of the old Kullu rajas, as a hotel. Rooms look down the Beas valley, and the Roerich estate, where the painter Nicholas Roerich lived from 1928 until his death in 1947, is a short uphill walk.

highlights.title: Fly from Billing to Bir
highlights.text: Tandem paragliding pilots launch from Billing at about 2,400 m and land in the tea fields of Bir, roughly 1,000 m lower. Flights last 15–30 minutes and cost around ₹3,000–4,500. India hosted its first Paragliding World Cup here in 2015.

highlights.title: Walk the Tirthan valley
highlights.text: The Great Himalayan National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2014, starts above the trout-river villages of Gushaini and Nagini. Day walks follow irrigation channels through kath-kuni hamlets; longer treks with a permit and a local guide reach alpine meadows.

highlights.title: Hear morning prayers in McLeodganj
highlights.text: The Tsuglagkhang complex, the Dalai Lama's temple, opens early, and monks debate in the courtyard of Namgyal Monastery most afternoons. Combine it with the Library of Tibetan Works and Archives lower down and the Norbulingka Institute's craft workshops near Sidhpur.

highlights.title: Eat apples where they grow
highlights.text: In September and October Kinnaur's orchards around Kalpa and Sangla are being picked and boxed. Stay in an orchard homestay, watch the Kinnaur Kailash peak turn pink at dawn from Kalpa, and drive to Chitkul, the last village on the Baspa road at 3,450 m.

money_savers: Book HRTC Volvo seats from Delhi on the HRTC online portal rather than through agents; the same seat often costs ₹200–400 more through a reseller.
Use HRTC ordinary buses between towns: Shimla to Manali costs roughly ₹450–650 against ₹5,000–7,000 for a taxi.
Take the ordinary Kalka–Shimla trains in second class for under ₹100; the scenery is identical to the chair-car trains.
Avoid Shimla and Manali in the Christmas–New Year week and mid-May to June, when room rates can double for the same room.
Order the thali or a plate of siddu at local dhabas instead of café menus; a filling meal costs ₹120–250.
In Kinnaur and Tirthan, homestays with dinner and breakfast included at ₹1,200–2,500 per person cost less than eating out every night.
getting_there: Most travellers start from Delhi. HRTC Volvo buses leave Kashmere Gate ISBT every evening for Shimla (≈ 350 km · 8–9 h), Manali (≈ 540 km · 12–14 h), Dharamshala (≈ 480 km · 10–12 h) and Bhuntar for Kasol and Tirthan. Trains run to Kalka, where you change to the toy train for Shimla, and to Chandigarh and Pathankot. Small airports at Shimla (Jubbarhatti), Bhuntar near Kullu and Gaggal near Dharamshala take flights from Delhi, but schedules are thin and weather cancellations are common, so keep a buffer day. Kinnaur is reached by road along the Sutlej from Shimla (≈ 220–240 km · 8–9 h to Kalpa or Sangla). Chamba is about 120 km from Pathankot and roughly 6 hours by road from Dharamshala.
permits: Indian travellers need no permit anywhere in this hive. Private vehicles going up to Rohtang Pass from Manali need an online permit from the district administration, with a daily cap on numbers; it is usually closed in winter. Treks into the core zone of the Great Himalayan National Park need a permit from the park office, normally arranged with a registered guide. Foreign nationals can visit Kalpa and Sangla freely but need an Inner Line Permit to continue towards Spiti beyond Jangi. Check current status before you travel.

months.weather: Shimla −2 to 9 °C, Manali −5 to 8 °C, snow spells
months.summary: Deep winter. Shimla and Manali usually get one or two good snowfalls, and Solang near Manali becomes a ski and snow-play slope. Roads to Kalpa stay open most days but freeze in the shade, and Chitkul is cut off after heavy snow. McLeodganj and Bir are cold and clear, with fewer visitors than any other month. Pack proper thermals and expect heaters to cost extra in budget rooms.
months.tip: If you want snow, book Manali with a flexible return; snowfall dates cannot be promised.

months.summary: Still wintry in the high towns, with late snow common in Manali and Shimla. Losar, the Tibetan New Year, often falls in February or early March, when McLeodganj's temples hold prayers and families visit each other. Bir and Chamba warm up first. Hotel prices stay low except on long weekends, and the toy train is pleasantly empty.
months.tip: Check the Losar date against the Tibetan calendar before you book; it moves every year.

months.summary: Spring arrives from the bottom up: rhododendrons flower in red on the Shimla and Dharamshala ridges, and Bir's paragliding season reopens with clear afternoons. Manali can still see snow early in the month. Kinnaur roads are open but HPTDC Kalpa usually reopens only after March. Students on exam break are not here yet, so rooms are fair.
months.tip: Carry a fleece and a rain shell; March days swing 15 °C between noon and night.

months.weather: Shimla 9 to 21 °C, Manali 5 to 20 °C, Kalpa 3 to 17 °C
months.summary: One of our two favourite months. Apple and apricot blossom in Kinnaur and Kullu, walks in Tirthan open up, and Kasol's cafés reopen after winter. Skies are mostly clear and crowds are still moderate before school holidays. The Bir flying season is in full swing. Higher trails such as Kheerganga still hold snow early in the month.
months.tip: Book Kalpa and Sangla for mid to late April to catch orchard blossom.

months.weather: Shimla 13 to 24 °C, Manali 9 to 24 °C, Chitkul 5 to 18 °C
months.summary: Peak plains-summer escape. Weather is excellent everywhere, but Shimla and Manali fill with families from mid-May and traffic queues form on the Mall Road approaches and at Solang. Go higher and further: Sangla and Chitkul, Tirthan, Chamba and Naggar stay calmer. Prices rise sharply in the big towns, so book early or stay outside them.
months.tip: Stay in Naggar or Old Manali instead of Mall Road to dodge May traffic.

months.weather: Shimla 15 to 25 °C, Manali 12 to 26 °C, pre-monsoon showers
months.summary: School holidays keep Shimla and Manali at full price until the monsoon reaches the hills, usually in the last week of June. The first half of the month is fine for Kinnaur, Kasol and Tirthan. GHNP treks open. Expect afternoon thunderstorms from mid-month and plan long drives for early mornings.
months.tip: Finish Kinnaur and Kullu road journeys before the monsoon sets in late June.

months.weather: Shimla 15 to 22 °C, heavy rain across Kullu and Kangra
months.summary: Monsoon month. Dharamshala is one of the wettest towns in India, Kullu sees landslides and river surges, and the Shimla–Kinnaur highway is often blocked for hours. Paragliding at Bir stops for the season. Chamba's Minjar Mela usually falls in late July or early August and is the reason to come. Otherwise we do not recommend travel this month.
months.tip: If you travel, keep two buffer days and follow HP disaster management alerts daily.

months.summary: The wettest stretch for most of the hive. Roads in the Beas valley and along the Sutlej suffer slides, and rivers run high and brown. The hills are green and empty, and hotel prices are at their lowest of the year. Minjar can stretch into early August. Avoid long road trips and river-side camping completely.
months.tip: Never camp on river banks in Kasol or Tirthan during monsoon; water rises fast at night.

months.summary: The rains usually ease by mid-September, roads are repaired, and the valleys are at their greenest. Apple harvest is busy in Kullu, Shimla district and Kinnaur, with trucks of boxed fruit on every highway. Bir's flying season restarts in late September. Prices are low until the Dussehra and Diwali holidays.
months.tip: Plan Kinnaur from the 20th onwards, once monsoon damage has usually been cleared.

months.weather: Shimla 10 to 20 °C, Manali 5 to 20 °C, clear skies
months.summary: Our other favourite month. Skies are clean after the monsoon, the Kinnaur Kailash and Dhauladhar peaks stand sharp, and Kullu Dussehra fills Dhalpur ground with village devtas for seven days. Bir has its steadiest flying weather. Puja and Diwali holidays bring crowds to Shimla and Manali for a week or two, so book those dates early.
months.tip: During Kullu Dussehra, stay in Naggar and ride in; Kullu town rooms sell out.

months.summary: Cold, dry and clear. Autumn colour in the Kullu orchards, long views from Kalpa and McLeodganj, and the lowest crowds of the good season. HPTDC Kalpa and many Chitkul guesthouses close by late November or December, and the first snow can arrive in the upper valleys. Excellent for Tirthan, Chamba, Bir and Shimla.
months.tip: Book Chitkul for early November at the latest; many places shut soon after.

months.summary: Quiet for three weeks, then the busiest week of the year as Christmas and New Year visitors fill Shimla and Manali hoping for snow. Christ Church in Shimla holds Christmas services. Early December is the best value of the whole year if you can live with cold nights. Kinnaur's higher villages are snowbound some days.
months.tip: Travel in the first half of December for low prices and empty roads.

faqs.q: How much does a Himachal trip cost per person?
faqs.a: On a saver budget, plan ₹1,800–3,000 a day for a hostel or shared HPTDC/homestay room, dhaba meals and HRTC buses, plus ₹1,800–3,800 for a return Delhi Volvo. A week therefore runs ₹15,000–25,000. Comfort trips with a private car and good hotels cost ₹7,000–12,000 a day each when two share. Signature stays at the Oberoi properties cost far more.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Himachal?
faqs.a: April to mid-June and late September to mid-November are the best months for most of this hive. Snow-seekers come in January and February for Manali and Shimla. July and August are monsoon months with landslides, and we advise against road trips then. October is excellent for clear views and Kullu Dussehra; April is best for orchard blossom.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Himachal?
faqs.a: Indian citizens need no permit for Shimla, Kullu, Kangra, Chamba or Kinnaur. Private vehicles to Rohtang Pass need an online permit, and treks into the core of the Great Himalayan National Park need a park permit. Foreign nationals need an Inner Line Permit only to continue from Kinnaur towards Spiti. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How do I get from Delhi to Manali cheaply?
faqs.a: Take an HRTC Volvo from Kashmere Gate ISBT in the evening; it reaches Manali in about 12–14 hours and costs roughly ₹1,500–1,900. HRTC ordinary buses are cheaper but slower and less comfortable. Book on the HRTC website a few days ahead in season. Private operators run similar coaches from Majnu ka Tilla, often at similar prices.

faqs.q: Is Himachal safe for solo women travellers?
faqs.a: Yes, Himachal is one of the more relaxed hill states for solo women, and hostels in Manali, Bir, Kasol and McLeodganj have women-only dorms. Use ordinary care: avoid isolated trails after dark, do not accept rides from strangers late at night, and tell your host your trekking plans. Party scenes in the Parvati valley are the main place to stay alert.

faqs.q: Will I get mobile network and ATMs in Himachal?
faqs.a: Jio, Airtel and BSNL work in all towns and most villages on main roads. Coverage thins inside the Great Himalayan National Park, above Pulga in the Parvati valley and around Chitkul, where BSNL and Jio are most reliable. ATMs are common in Shimla, Manali, Dharamshala, Kullu, Chamba and Reckong Peo; carry cash for villages, where UPI may fail on weak signal.

faqs.q: Is Himachal good for a trip with kids or seniors?
faqs.a: Yes. Shimla, Naggar, McLeodganj and Chamba sit between 1,000 and 2,200 m, roads are paved and medical care is reasonable in the district towns. The toy train is a hit with children. Keep long drives to 5–6 hours a day, avoid monsoon months, and for Chitkul at 3,450 m talk to your doctor if anyone has heart or lung conditions.

faqs.q: Are roads in Himachal open in winter?
faqs.a: The main highways to Shimla, Manali, Dharamshala, Chamba and Kalpa stay open in winter, though snow can close them for a day or two and black ice is common in the mornings. Rohtang Pass closes for vehicles in winter, while the Atal Tunnel stays open except in heavy snow. Chitkul and the higher Kinnaur roads are often blocked after snowfall. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many days do I need for Himachal?
faqs.a: Six nights covers one circuit well, such as Shimla, Naggar and Manali, or McLeodganj, Bir and Chamba. Eight to ten nights lets you add Kinnaur or the Tirthan valley without long drives every day. Distances look short on the map but mountain roads average 25–35 km an hour, so plan one long road day for every two or three rest days.
